questions.question: Which country has the most time zones?
questions.fun_fact: France has 12 time zones thanks to its overseas territories — more than any other country, even Russia with 11.

questions.question: Which city gets more rainfall: London or Sydney?
questions.fun_fact: Sydney receives around 1,200 mm of rain per year, while London gets only about 600 mm. London's reputation as a rainy city is greatly exaggerated.

questions.question: Which country has the most lakes in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Canada holds over 60% of all lakes in the world — more than all other countries combined.

questions.question: Which city is the highest administrative capital in the world by altitude above sea level?
questions.fun_fact: La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, sits at about 3,640 metres above sea level. Water boils there at around 87°C, making cooking take significantly longer.

questions.question: Which African country was never a European colony?
questions.fun_fact: Ethiopia defeated the Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 and remained one of the few African countries to stay fully independent throughout the colonial era.

questions.question: Which country recently surpassed China to become the world's most populous?
questions.fun_fact: India overtook China in 2023 with over 1.4 billion people. The Indian state of Uttar Pradesh alone has more inhabitants than Brazil.

questions.question: Which river is longer: the Nile or the Amazon?

answers.text: It's disputed — both are roughly equal

questions.fun_fact: Depending on measurement method and source definition, both have been declared the world's longest river. Newer measurements favour the Amazon; traditionally the Nile held the title.

questions.question: What is the capital of Myanmar?
questions.fun_fact: Naypyidaw became the capital in 2005 and is a nearly deserted planned city featuring 20-lane highways with almost no traffic.

questions.question: Which two countries are tied for bordering the most other countries (14 each)?
questions.fun_fact: China and Russia each border 14 countries, jointly holding the world record. Brazil leads South America with 10 neighbours.

questions.question: Which lake is the deepest in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Lake Baikal in Siberia is 1,642 metres deep and contains about 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

questions.question: Which country contains the driest place on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Parts of the Atacama Desert in Chile have never recorded rainfall. Some areas resemble Mars so closely that NASA tests rovers there.

questions.question: Which two countries in the world are each entirely surrounded by Italy?
questions.fun_fact: Both San Marino and Vatican City are completely enclaved by Italy. Lesotho is also an enclave nation, but it sits within South Africa.

questions.question: Which continent has the most countries?
questions.fun_fact: Africa has 54 recognised states — more than any other continent. Many of these borders were drawn by colonial powers using a ruler on a map.

questions.question: What is the largest island in the world that is not its own continent?
questions.fun_fact: Greenland covers 2.16 million km² but has only around 56,000 inhabitants. It belongs politically to Denmark but geographically lies in North America.

questions.question: Which desert is the largest in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Antarctica is technically a desert, receiving less than 250 mm of precipitation per year. At 14 million km² it is larger than the Sahara.

questions.question: Which European country has the lowest population density?
questions.fun_fact: Iceland has only about 3.5 inhabitants per square kilometre — one of the lowest densities in Europe.

questions.question: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Canada's coastline stretches over 202,000 km. Walking it at 8 hours per day would take more than 19 years.

questions.question: Which mountain continues to grow taller every year?
questions.fun_fact: Mount Everest grows about 4 mm per year due to the tectonic collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates.

questions.question: Which country is shaped like a boot?
questions.fun_fact: Italy's boot shape is so distinctive it's one of the most recognisable countries on any world map. Sicily is the 'ball' the boot is kicking.

questions.question: Which country produces the most coffee in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Brazil produces about one third of the world's coffee. In 2021, an unusual frost destroyed so many coffee plants in Brazil that prices rose globally.

questions.question: Which US state was purchased from Russia?
questions.fun_fact: The USA bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million — about 2 cents per hectare. Critics at the time called it 'Seward's Icebox'.

questions.question: Which famous observatory marks the Prime Meridian dividing the eastern and western hemispheres?
questions.fun_fact: The Prime Meridian was fixed at Greenwich, London in 1884. You can literally stand with one foot in the East and one in the West on its brass line.

questions.question: Which country has the most active volcanoes?
questions.fun_fact: Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire and has about 130 active volcanoes. The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was so loud it was heard nearly 5,000 km away.

questions.question: Which two continents are separated by the Bosphorus?
questions.fun_fact: Istanbul is the only major city in the world that spans two continents. Millions of people commute between Europe and Asia by ferry every day.

questions.question: Which country officially renamed itself in April 2018?
questions.fun_fact: King Mswati III announced the change on Swaziland's 50th independence anniversary. North Macedonia's rename only took effect in February 2019, and Czechia adopted its short name back in 2016.

questions.question: Which country has more than 17,000 islands?
questions.fun_fact: Indonesia consists of over 17,500 islands, of which only about 6,000 are inhabited. It stretches over 5,000 km — as wide as Lisbon to Moscow.

questions.question: Which European country has no university?
questions.fun_fact: Vatican City has the Vatican Library and the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, but no university in the traditional sense. With around 800 residents, it is the world's smallest state.

questions.question: Which country has the greatest north-to-south length on its mainland?
questions.fun_fact: Chile stretches over 4,300 km from north to south but averages only 177 km in width. It ranges from the Atacama Desert in the north to near-Antarctic fjords in the south.

questions.question: Which European city is currently divided and serves as the capital of two separate political entities?
questions.fun_fact: Nicosia in Cyprus is the last divided capital in Europe. The northern part is the capital of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus; the south is the capital of the Republic of Cyprus.

questions.question: Which country has the most pyramids?
questions.fun_fact: Sudan has over 200 pyramids — nearly twice as many as Egypt. The Nubian pyramids at Meroë are smaller but far more numerous, and far less well known.

questions.question: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fun_fact: Although 71% of Earth is covered in water, over 96% of it is salt water. Only a tiny fraction is available as fresh drinking water.

questions.question: Which is the largest island nation in the world by area?
questions.fun_fact: Indonesia covers about 1.9 million km² across more than 17,000 islands, making it larger than every European country except Russia.

questions.question: What is the lowest point on Earth's land surface?
questions.fun_fact: The surface of the Dead Sea sits about 430 metres below sea level and sinks further each year. Its salt content is so high you cannot sink in it.

questions.question: Which country uses a single time zone despite spanning five geographic ones?
questions.fun_fact: All of China runs on UTC+8 (Beijing Time). At the Afghan border, clocks jump 3.5 hours; Russia by contrast uses 11 different time zones.

questions.question: Which city has the largest population in the world (metro area)?
questions.fun_fact: Greater Tokyo has over 37 million inhabitants — more than all of Canada. Its rail system transports around 40 million passengers per day.

questions.question: Which country lies in all four hemispheres at once?
questions.fun_fact: The island nation of Kiribati straddles both the Equator and the International Date Line, placing it in the northern, southern, eastern, and western hemispheres.

questions.question: What is the longest mountain range in the world?
questions.fun_fact: The Andes stretch over 7,000 km along South America's west coast through seven countries. The longest range overall is the Mid-Ocean Ridge beneath the sea.

questions.question: Which country is home to the largest English-speaking population in Africa?
questions.fun_fact: Nigeria has over 220 million inhabitants and English is the official language, used in government, education, and media. Estimates put English speakers there at 60-100 million.

questions.question: Which is the smallest of the world's five oceans by area?
questions.fun_fact: The Arctic Ocean covers about 14 million km² — roughly one tenth the size of the Pacific. It is mostly frozen in winter.

questions.question: Which European country has the most saunas per capita?
questions.fun_fact: Finland has around 3.3 million saunas for 5.5 million people — almost one sauna for every two Finns. There are even saunas in parliament buildings and a Burger King.

questions.question: Which German state borders the most other German states?
questions.fun_fact: Lower Saxony borders nine other German states: Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Hesse, and North Rhine-Westphalia.

questions.question: Which country gifted the Statue of Liberty to the USA?
questions.fun_fact: The Statue of Liberty arrived in 350 pieces by ship from France in 1885. The head was displayed at world exhibitions in Paris for years beforehand.

questions.question: Which country has a flag that is not rectangular?
questions.fun_fact: Nepal's flag consists of two stacked triangles and is the only non-rectangular national flag in the world. Switzerland's flag is square but still has four sides.

questions.question: Which country has no official capital?
questions.fun_fact: The Pacific island nation of Nauru has no official capital. Government operations are based in the Yaren district. At 21 km², Nauru is the third smallest country in the world.

questions.question: Which European capital was built on 14 islands?
questions.fun_fact: Stockholm spans 14 islands connected by 57 bridges. The old town Gamla Stan stands on the island of Stadsholmen and was founded in the 13th century.

questions.question: Which country renamed its capital in 2019?
questions.fun_fact: Kazakhstan renamed its capital Nur-Sultan in 2019 to honour outgoing president Nursultan Nazarbayev, then reversed the decision back to Astana in 2022.

questions.question: Which river flows through the most European capitals?
questions.fun_fact: The Danube flows through four European capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. No other river in the world links so many capital cities.

questions.question: If you travel due south from Detroit, Michigan, which country do you enter first?
questions.fun_fact: Windsor, Ontario sits directly south of Detroit because the Detroit River bends so the Canadian shore lies below the US one — the only place along the US-Canada border where this happens.

questions.question: Which African country's name translates to 'Lion Mountains'?
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named the coastline 'Serra Leoa' in 1462, supposedly because the mountains' silhouette or the thunder rolling over them reminded him of lions.

questions.question: At Triple Point in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany, what can a visitor do in a single step?

answers.text: Stand in three countries at once
Cross three time zones at once

questions.fun_fact: The Vaalserberg hilltop near Aachen marks the tripoint where the three borders meet, and a small concrete marker lets you place feet in all three nations simultaneously.

questions.question: Which African country is almost entirely surrounded by Senegal?
questions.fun_fact: The Gambia is a narrow ribbon of land hugging the Gambia River, bordered by Senegal on all sides except for a short Atlantic coastline. Its shape comes from how far British gunboats could shell upriver in colonial negotiations.

questions.question: Russia and which other country share a maritime border less than 4 km wide?
questions.fun_fact: Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (USA) sit in the Bering Strait about 3.8 km apart, with the International Date Line running between them — locals call them Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Island.

questions.question: The town of Büsingen am Hochrhein is German territory entirely surrounded by which country?
questions.fun_fact: Büsingen uses the Swiss franc, has a Swiss postcode in addition to its German one, and its football team plays in the Swiss league — but legally it is part of Baden-Württemberg.

questions.question: On which continent does the Nile river have its source?
questions.fun_fact: The Nile rises from tributaries feeding Lake Victoria in East Africa and flows north for around 6,650 km before reaching the Mediterranean — one of the few major rivers in the world that flows northward.

questions.question: Which Belgian-Dutch border town has houses where the front door and the kitchen can be in different countries?
questions.fun_fact: Baarle contains 22 Belgian enclaves inside the Netherlands, some with Dutch counter-enclaves inside them. White crosses with B and NL letters mark the border across streets and even down hallways.

questions.question: Which is the only sea on Earth with no coastline?
questions.fun_fact: The Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic is defined by ocean currents — the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic, Canary, and North Atlantic Equatorial currents — rather than by land, and is famous for floating mats of Sargassum seaweed.

questions.question: Roughly a quarter of which country's land lies below sea level?
questions.fun_fact: About 26% of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and over 60% of the population lives in flood-prone areas. Centuries of polders, dikes, and pumping — once windmill-powered, now electric — keep them dry.

questions.question: The Caspian Sea is technically what?

answers.text: An arm of the Black Sea
A part of the Arctic Ocean

questions.fun_fact: The Caspian is fully enclosed by land and holds about 78,000 cubic km of water — more than all the American Great Lakes combined — though its legal status as 'sea' was negotiated by the five bordering states for oil rights.

questions.question: Which country owns Easter Island?
questions.fun_fact: Easter Island lies more than 3,500 km west of mainland Chile, making it one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world. Its nearest inhabited neighbour, Pitcairn, is still over 2,000 km away.

questions.question: Which mountain's summit is the point on Earth's surface farthest from Earth's centre?
questions.fun_fact: Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo's 6,263 m summit sits about 2 km farther from the planet's centre than Everest's 8,849 m peak — making it the closest spot on Earth to outer space.

questions.question: Which African lake forms the border of four countries?
questions.fun_fact: Lake Tanganyika borders Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is also the world's longest freshwater lake at around 670 km from end to end.

questions.question: Lesotho is unusual because it is entirely surrounded by one other country. Which one?
questions.fun_fact: Lesotho is the world's only independent state where every point of land lies above 1,000 m, earning it the nickname 'Kingdom in the Sky'. It even gets occasional snow in winter.

questions.question: Which African country also has territory in Asia via the Sinai Peninsula?
questions.fun_fact: Egypt's Sinai Peninsula sits on the Asian side of the Suez Canal, while Cairo and the bulk of the country lie in Africa — making Egypt the famous example of an Afro-Asian transcontinental country.

questions.question: Which Asian country drives on the left side of the road?
questions.fun_fact: Japan adopted left-hand traffic in the 19th century partly under British influence on its early railways. About one third of the world drives on the left — most of them former British territories.

questions.question: Which sea has been shrinking dramatically since the 1960s due to irrigation diversions?
questions.fun_fact: Once the world's fourth-largest lake, the Aral Sea lost over 90% of its volume after Soviet engineers diverted its source rivers to cotton fields, leaving stranded fishing boats in a desert of toxic salt.

questions.question: Iceland is being pulled apart by two tectonic plates. Which two?
questions.fun_fact: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs straight through Iceland, separating the plates by roughly 2 cm per year. At Þingvellir National Park visitors can walk and even snorkel between the two continents.

questions.question: Which country is the only one in the world named after a woman?
questions.fun_fact: The Caribbean island Saint Lucia is named after Saint Lucy of Syracuse. The country also has the unusual distinction of changing colonial hands between France and Britain 14 times.

questions.question: What direction does the Amazon River flow today?
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon now flows eastward into the Atlantic, but geologists believe that before the Andes rose roughly 10 million years ago it ran the opposite way, draining westward into the Pacific.

questions.question: Which European country contains the geographically deepest cave on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Veryovkina Cave in Georgia's Abkhazia region has been explored to more than 2,200 m below the surface — deep enough to swallow seven Eiffel Towers stacked on each other.

questions.question: Which island is split between three countries?
questions.fun_fact: Borneo is shared by Indonesia (Kalimantan), Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak), and the tiny sultanate of Brunei. New Guinea, by contrast, is split between only two countries.

questions.question: What is unusual about the country of Andorra's head of state?

answers.text: It has two heads of state, one of whom is the French president
Its monarch is elected for life
Its president must speak Catalan and Basque

questions.fun_fact: Andorra is a co-principality dating from 1278: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain serve jointly as heads of state — the only country where a foreign elected leader holds the top office ex officio.

questions.question: Which body of water lies between Saudi Arabia and Africa?
questions.fun_fact: The Red Sea is gradually widening as the Arabian and African plates pull apart — geologists expect it to eventually become a full ocean over millions of years.

questions.question: Which country contains the Door to Hell, a natural gas crater that has been burning continuously since 1971?
questions.fun_fact: Soviet geologists set the Darvaza gas crater alight to burn off methane, expecting it to die in days. More than 50 years later it still glows; Turkmenistan's president has repeatedly ordered it extinguished.

questions.question: Which is the world's largest country that lies entirely south of the equator?
questions.fun_fact: Brazil is bigger overall but straddles the equator. Australia covers roughly 7.7 million km² wholly in the southern hemisphere — and its widest east-west extent is greater than the distance from London to Moscow.

questions.question: Cabinda is an oil-rich exclave belonging to which country?
questions.fun_fact: Cabinda is separated from the rest of Angola by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo that reaches the Atlantic. The exclave produces the majority of Angola's offshore oil.

questions.question: Which strait separates Spain from Africa at its narrowest point?
questions.fun_fact: At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide. On a clear day you can easily see Morocco from southern Spain, and ferries cross in roughly an hour.

questions.question: Which country has a section of its territory that can only be reached by land by crossing another country?
questions.fun_fact: To drive from the contiguous United States to Alaska you must cross Canada. Point Roberts in Washington State is another famous US example — a peninsula hanging south of the 49th parallel, reachable by road only through Canada.

questions.question: Which European city's old town sits on an island in a river surrounded by canals?
questions.fun_fact: Strasbourg's Grande Île is an island formed by two arms of the river Ill and is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Petite France quarter on its western tip is laced with half-timbered houses overhanging the canals.

questions.question: What is unusual about the borders of the US state of Michigan?

answers.text: It is split into two separate peninsulas
It has more than ten panhandles

questions.fun_fact: Michigan's Upper and Lower Peninsulas are connected only by the Mackinac Bridge across the Straits of Mackinac. Until the bridge opened in 1957, the two halves were linked solely by ferry.

questions.question: Which river forms much of the natural border between the USA and Mexico?
questions.fun_fact: The Rio Grande follows the border for about 2,000 km from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico. When the river shifts course, small patches of land have historically swapped sides between the two countries.

questions.question: Which country contains the westernmost point of mainland Europe?
questions.fun_fact: Cabo da Roca in Portugal is the westernmost point of continental Europe. A stone marker quotes the poet Camões: 'Here, where the land ends and the sea begins.'

questions.question: Which of these countries lies furthest north?
questions.fun_fact: Reykjavík sits at about 64° N, north of any major Estonian or Scottish city. Iceland's northernmost island, Grímsey, is crossed by the Arctic Circle itself.

questions.question: What geological feature is the East African Rift slowly creating?
questions.fun_fact: The African continent is splitting along a fault stretching from the Afar region to Mozambique. Over millions of years the Horn of Africa is expected to drift away, forming a new ocean basin.

questions.question: Which Pacific archipelago has the only equatorial penguin species?
questions.fun_fact: The Galápagos penguin survives on the equator because the cold Humboldt and Cromwell currents wrap the islands in unusually chilly water. It is the only penguin found naturally in the northern hemisphere.

questions.question: What is the most striking feature of the country of Chad's Lake Chad?

answers.text: It has shrunk by more than 90% since the 1960s
It is the world's deepest tropical lake

questions.fun_fact: Climate change and irrigation have shrunk Lake Chad from around 26,000 km² in the 1960s to under 1,500 km², gutting fisheries for Chad, Niger, Nigeria, and Cameroon.

questions.question: Which country is shaped like a giant question mark, including a long thin tail?
questions.fun_fact: Thailand's southern peninsula tapers into a thin strip down the Malay Peninsula, giving the country its characteristic outline. At its narrowest, the Kra Isthmus is only about 44 km wide.

questions.question: Which country is home to the largest tropical rainforest in the world?
questions.fun_fact: About 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil, with the rest spread across eight other countries and one territory. The forest hosts an estimated 10% of all species known on Earth.

questions.question: What is the only US state whose capital is not connected to the rest of the country by a road?
questions.fun_fact: Juneau is surrounded by mountains, icefields, and ocean. The only ways in or out are by boat or plane — there is no highway linking it to the rest of Alaska or the lower 48.

questions.question: Which African country is split almost exactly in half by the equator?
questions.fun_fact: The equator crosses Gabon just north of its capital, Libreville. Several African countries straddle the line, but Gabon and São Tomé and Príncipe sit closest to centred on it.

questions.question: What geographic distinction does the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu hold?

answers.text: Its highest point is only about 4.5 m above sea level
It has the world's longest coral reef
It contains the deepest oceanic trench

questions.fun_fact: Tuvalu is so low-lying that king tides regularly flood streets in the capital, Funafuti. Climate change has made it a frequent symbol of nations threatened by rising seas.

questions.question: Which European country is home to the world's deepest underground railway station?
questions.fun_fact: Kyiv's Arsenalna metro station sits about 105 m below ground — partly because it was tunnelled through a steep riverbank above the Dnieper, and partly to double as a Cold War shelter.

questions.question: Which South American capital city sits on the equator?
questions.fun_fact: Quito is the closest capital city to the equator, with the line passing just north of the city. Ecuador is even named for it — 'Ecuador' is Spanish for 'equator'.

questions.question: Which country has more islands than any other in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Sweden has roughly 267,000 islands when small skerries are counted — far more than Indonesia's better-known archipelago. Most are uninhabited rocks in the Baltic.

questions.question: Which country has overseas territory in South America, the Caribbean, the Pacific, AND the Indian Ocean?
questions.fun_fact: France holds territories in South America (French Guiana), the Caribbean (Martinique, Guadeloupe), the Pacific (New Caledonia, French Polynesia), the Indian Ocean (Mayotte, Réunion), and even North America (Saint-Pierre and Miquelon).

questions.question: Which country has the unusual claim of being entirely above 1,000 m elevation?
questions.fun_fact: Lesotho's lowest point — at the junction of the Orange and Makhaleng rivers — is about 1,400 m above sea level. No other independent country has so high a low point.

questions.question: Which lake straddles the border between Switzerland, Germany, and Austria?
questions.fun_fact: Lake Constance has no formally defined border on the open water between the three countries — they have never reached a treaty fixing the lines, leaving the middle of the lake as a sort of legal grey zone.

questions.question: If you sail due south from the southern tip of Africa, what is the first continent you reach?
questions.fun_fact: From the Cape of Good Hope, the only landmass directly south across the Southern Ocean is Antarctica, around 4,000 km away. The latitudes between are nicknamed the 'Roaring Forties' for their fierce westerly winds.

questions.question: Which city lies farther west: Reno, Nevada or Los Angeles, California?

answers.text: They sit at the same longitude

questions.fun_fact: Reno sits at about 119.8° W while Los Angeles is near 118.2° W, so Reno is roughly 160 km farther west — California's coastline actually curves back eastward as it runs south toward Los Angeles.

questions.question: If you stand in the Spanish town of Llívia, you are in Spanish territory completely surrounded by which country?
questions.fun_fact: Llívia became a Spanish exclave by a quirk of the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees: the deal ceded 'villages' to France, but Llívia was legally a town, so Spain kept it — leaving it stranded a few kilometres inside France.

questions.question: Which US state contains the point of the lower 48 states closest to the continent of Africa?
questions.fun_fact: Quoddy Head in eastern Maine is the easternmost point of the contiguous United States, and its far-northeast position makes it the closest mainland US spot to Africa's northwest coast — nearer than anywhere in Florida, even though Florida lies much farther south.

questions.question: Why is the ocean blue?

answers.text: Water itself absorbs red light and scatters blue
It simply reflects the colour of the sky
Blue algae tint the water across the globe

questions.fun_fact: Pure water is faintly blue even in a deep bathtub. Water molecules absorb longer red wavelengths, so the light that survives to bounce back is blue — the sky's reflection only adds a little on top.

questions.question: What makes desert sand dunes 'sing' or boom as they move?

answers.text: Avalanching sand grains vibrating in unison
Wind whistling through buried rock crevices
Trapped underground gas escaping the dune

questions.fun_fact: When sand of just the right size and dryness slides down a dune face, the grains shear past each other in sync, producing a low droning hum that can reach 105 decibels and be heard kilometres away.

questions.question: Why does the Dead Sea let swimmers float so easily?

answers.text: Its extreme salt content makes the water denser than the body
Underground gas bubbles push bathers upward
Its unusually cold water is far denser than warm seawater

questions.fun_fact: The Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than the ocean. That dissolved salt makes the water denser than a human body, so you bob on the surface like a cork rather than swimming through it.

questions.question: What causes the salt flats of Bolivia to act like a giant mirror after rain?

answers.text: A thin sheet of water over a perfectly flat salt crust
Reflective salt crystals that polish themselves smooth
A layer of mercury beneath the salt surface

questions.fun_fact: When a shallow film of rainwater sits on the Salar de Uyuni, the salt below is so flat that the water has nowhere to pool or ripple, turning the whole plain into the world's largest natural mirror reflecting the sky.

questions.question: Why does a geyser like Old Faithful erupt in regular bursts rather than flowing steadily?

answers.text: Trapped water superheats until it flashes to steam and blasts out
An underground pump cycles the water on and off
Tides far below ground squeeze the water upward

questions.fun_fact: In a geyser's narrow plumbing, water deep down stays liquid above 100°C under pressure. Once it finally boils, the sudden expansion to steam ejects the column above it, then the chamber refills and the cycle repeats.

questions.question: What makes a rainforest produce much of its own rainfall?

answers.text: Trees release water vapour that forms clouds and rain
The canopy is cold enough to condense passing sea fog
Rivers evaporate faster under the dense tree cover

questions.fun_fact: Amazon trees pump enormous amounts of moisture into the air through their leaves. This 'transpiration' seeds clouds, so a single water molecule can fall as rain, be re-released by a tree, and fall again several times across the basin.

questions.question: Why is fresh snow such a brilliant white when the ice it's made of is clear?

answers.text: Countless tiny crystal facets scatter all colours of light equally
Snow contains microscopic white mineral dust
Frozen air bubbles glow white in sunlight

questions.fun_fact: A single ice crystal is transparent, but a snowdrift is a jumble of millions of them. Light bounces off all those surfaces in every direction, and since no colour is absorbed more than another, the pile looks white.

questions.question: Why does the air get colder as you climb a mountain, even though you're nearer the Sun?

answers.text: Thinner high air holds less heat and expands as it rises
Mountain peaks block the Sun's warming rays
Snow on the summit cools the surrounding air

questions.fun_fact: Air is warmed mainly from the ground up, not directly by sunlight. As you go higher the air thins and any rising parcel expands and cools, dropping roughly 6.5°C for every kilometre of altitude.

questions.question: What causes the Northern Lights to glow in the sky?

answers.text: Charged particles from the Sun striking atoms in the upper atmosphere
Sunlight refracting through high-altitude ice clouds
Reflections of city lights off the polar ice cap

questions.fun_fact: The aurora's colours reveal which gas is glowing: oxygen high up gives green and red, while nitrogen produces blues and purples. The same particle storms can also disrupt satellites and power grids.

questions.question: Why does the Moon pull ocean tides up on both sides of the Earth at once?

answers.text: The Moon pulls the near ocean and the far ocean lags behind
The Moon's light heats and expands the seas on both sides
The Sun fills in the bulge opposite the Moon

questions.fun_fact: Gravity tugs the near-side ocean toward the Moon, but the solid Earth gets pulled away from the far-side ocean, leaving a second bulge behind. That's why most coasts get two high tides a day, not one.

questions.question: Why does a beach feel cooler than the inland on a hot summer afternoon?

answers.text: Cooler air flows in from the sea as warm land air rises
Sea spray physically chills the surrounding air
Coastal sand reflects almost all of the Sun's heat

questions.fun_fact: Land heats up far faster than water. The hot air over the land rises, and cooler air sitting over the sea rushes in to replace it, creating the refreshing onshore breeze that beachgoers feel by midday.

questions.question: What makes quicksand so dangerous to step into?

answers.text: Water-saturated sand loses its firmness and can't bear weight
It actively sucks objects down toward the centre of the Earth
Hidden currents drag anything that lands on it sideways

questions.fun_fact: Quicksand is just ordinary sand whose grains are floated apart by upward-seeping water, so it can't support weight. You actually can't sink fully under because your body is less dense than the slurry — the danger is getting stuck as the tide rises.

questions.question: Why does sea ice, made from salty ocean water, taste only faintly salty?

answers.text: Salt is squeezed out as the water freezes
Ocean salt evaporates away before the ice forms
Only freshwater rivers freeze on the ocean surface

questions.fun_fact: When seawater freezes, the crystal structure of ice rejects the salt, pushing it into briny pockets that gradually drain out. Old sea ice becomes fresh enough that polar explorers have melted it for drinking water.

questions.question: Why do most of the world's great deserts sit near the same latitudes north and south of the equator?

answers.text: Air that rose at the equator sinks there, dry and rainless
Those bands are simply the farthest from any ocean
The Sun lingers longest over those exact latitudes

questions.fun_fact: Warm equatorial air rises and dumps its rain, then drifts and descends around 30° north and south. Sinking air warms and dries out, which is why the Sahara, Arabian, and Australian deserts all cluster along those belts.

questions.question: What gives the Grand Canyon's rock layers their many different colours?

answers.text: Different minerals, especially iron, in each rock layer
Sunlight hitting the walls at changing angles
Algae growing in coloured bands on the cliffs

questions.fun_fact: Each band marks a different ancient environment. Iron is the main painter: oxidised iron makes reds and oranges, while greener and grey layers formed where there was less oxygen, so the canyon walls read like a colour-coded timeline.

questions.question: Why does a river bend more and more sharply over time instead of running straight?

answers.text: Water erodes the outer bank and deposits sand on the inner one
Rivers always follow underground magnetic lines
The planet's rotation forces all rivers into curves

questions.fun_fact: On a bend, water moves faster on the outside and chews away the bank, while it slows on the inside and drops sediment. This lopsided action exaggerates the curve until loops sometimes pinch off into oxbow lakes.

questions.question: Why is the air at the bottom of a deep valley sometimes colder at night than higher up the slopes?

answers.text: Cold dense air drains downhill and pools at the bottom
Valley floors are always closer to underground ice
Sunlight never reaches the valley floor at all

questions.fun_fact: On clear, still nights the ground chills the air touching it, and because cold air is heavier it slides down the slopes and collects on the valley floor. These 'frost hollows' can be several degrees colder than the hillsides above.

questions.question: What makes a hot spring hot in the first place?

answers.text: Water seeps down to hot rock and rises back up heated
Sunlight concentrated by surrounding pale rocks
Friction from the water flowing through narrow cracks

questions.fun_fact: Rainwater trickles deep underground, gets warmed by hot rock or nearby magma, then buoyantly rises back to the surface. In volcanic regions the water can emerge near boiling, and it often carries dissolved minerals that build colourful terraces.

questions.question: Why do clouds, full of tonnes of water, float instead of falling?

answers.text: Their droplets are tiny and rising warm air holds them up
Water vapour is naturally lighter than the air below
Static electricity suspends the droplets in place

questions.fun_fact: A cloud's water is split into droplets so small that air resistance lets them drift down at a crawl, and gentle updrafts easily keep them aloft. Only when droplets merge into raindrops do they finally grow heavy enough to fall.

questions.question: Why does the sea look like it has a sharp 'edge' at the horizon?

answers.text: The Earth curves away beyond a certain distance
A wall of denser air blocks the view past it
Sunlight can only travel a fixed distance over water

questions.fun_fact: Because the planet is round, the surface drops away from your line of sight. For someone standing on the shore the horizon sits only about 5 km off — climb a cliff or a ship's mast and that edge retreats much farther.

questions.question: What makes a glacier flow downhill like an extremely slow river?

answers.text: Its own weight makes the ice deform and slide
Wind pushes the ice steadily down the valley
Meltwater freezes behind it and shoves it forward

questions.fun_fact: Under the immense pressure of its own mass, glacial ice behaves a bit like putty, deforming internally while meltwater at its base lets it slide. Some glaciers creep along at only a few centimetres a day.

questions.question: Why does a flat, snow-free road sometimes shimmer with a fake 'puddle' on a hot day?

answers.text: Light bends through a layer of hot air near the surface
Heat melts a thin film of tar that reflects the sky
Rising steam from the road condenses into a mirage

questions.fun_fact: A blazing road heats the air just above it, and light passing from cooler air into that hot layer bends upward. Your eye traces it back as a patch of sky on the ground — the same mirage that fools desert travellers with imaginary lakes.

questions.question: Why does the temperature deep inside a cave stay almost the same all year round?

answers.text: Thick rock insulates it from surface weather
Caves are heated by a steady flow of warm groundwater
Trapped air can't move, so it never changes temperature

questions.fun_fact: Surrounding rock is a poor conductor and a huge heat store, so deep caves hover close to the local yearly average temperature whatever the season. That stability is why caves were prized for storing food and ageing cheese and wine.

questions.question: What makes the water of a tropical lagoon look such a vivid turquoise?

answers.text: Shallow water over pale sand reflects blue-green light back up
Dissolved copper minerals dye the water turquoise
A surface film of plankton scatters green light

questions.fun_fact: In shallow water the seabed of white coral sand bounces sunlight back before deep water can swallow the blue-green wavelengths. Over a dark or deep bottom the very same sea would instead look a far darker blue.

questions.question: The country of Ecuador takes its name from what?
questions.fun_fact: 'Ecuador' is simply the Spanish word for equator. It is the only country in the world named after a line of latitude rather than a person, place, or feature.

questions.question: How did the Pacific Ocean get its name?

answers.text: Magellan found it unusually calm and peaceful
It was named after a Spanish ship, the Pacífica
It comes from a Polynesian word for vast

questions.fun_fact: Magellan called it 'Mar Pacífico' (peaceful sea) in 1520 after surviving the stormy strait at South America's tip and finding the waters beyond eerily calm. The name stuck despite the Pacific's many typhoons.

questions.question: The Canary Islands were named after what?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Latin 'Canariae Insulae', meaning 'Islands of the Dogs', possibly after large dogs found there by the Romans. The canary bird is named after the islands, not the other way around.

questions.question: Why is Greenland called 'green' when it is mostly ice?

answers.text: Erik the Red picked the name to attract settlers
Its southern coast was once a lush jungle
It is a mistranslation of an old Norse word for ice

questions.fun_fact: Erik the Red, banished from Iceland, named the icy island 'Greenland' around 982 AD specifically because an appealing name would lure colonists. It may be history's earliest recorded real-estate marketing spin.

questions.question: The name 'America' honours Amerigo Vespucci. What was unusual about how it was applied?

answers.text: A mapmaker added it for South America without Vespucci's knowledge
Vespucci personally paid to have it named after him
It was originally the name of his ship

questions.fun_fact: German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller printed 'America' on a 1507 map, crediting Vespucci for recognising it as a new continent. He later regretted it and removed the name, but it had already caught on across Europe.

questions.question: Which sea is named after a man who, by legend, drowned in it?
questions.fun_fact: In Greek myth, King Aegeus threw himself into the sea after wrongly believing his son Theseus had died fighting the Minotaur, because Theseus forgot to swap his black sails for white ones.

questions.question: The Indian Ocean is unusual among the major oceans because it is named after what?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only ocean named after a single nation, India. The others take their names from a Greek titan (Atlantic), calmness (Pacific), the far north (Arctic), and the southern pole (Southern).

questions.question: The country name 'Pakistan' was created in 1933 in what way?

answers.text: As an acronym from the names of its regions
By translating an ancient Sanskrit prayer
By a vote among British colonial officers

questions.fun_fact: A student named Choudhry Rahmat Ali coined it from Punjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan, while it also conveniently means 'land of the pure' in Persian and Urdu.

questions.question: Why does the African country Cameroon carry a name meaning 'shrimp'?

answers.text: Portuguese sailors found a river full of shrimp
Its coastline is shaped like a shrimp
Shrimp was its main export to Europe

questions.fun_fact: In 1472 Portuguese explorers named the Wouri estuary 'Rio dos Camarões' (River of Shrimp) after the swarms of ghost shrimp they saw. The whole country eventually took its name from that river.

questions.question: The US state of Rhode Island is thought to be named after a comparison to which Mediterranean island?
questions.fun_fact: An explorer's likening of an island in Narragansett Bay to the Greek isle of Rhodes is one leading theory. Ironically, Rhode Island is the smallest US state and its mainland is not an island at all.

questions.question: The word 'continent' originally comes from a Latin phrase meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: It derives from 'terra continens', meaning 'continuous land' — a stretch of ground held together without a break. The same Latin root gives us the everyday word 'contain'.

questions.question: How did Brazil get its name?

answers.text: From a red dyewood tree harvested there
From a Portuguese explorer named Brazão
From a native word meaning sunshine

questions.fun_fact: Brazil is named after brazilwood, a tree yielding a prized red dye that was the colony's first major export. The country was effectively named after a commodity rather than a person or place.

questions.question: The Strait of Magellan is named after the explorer, but who actually completed the first circumnavigation he began?

answers.text: His crew, after Magellan died mid-voyage
A rival captain who finished it decades later

questions.fun_fact: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, so he never personally circled the globe. His captain Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship home in 1522, completing the first lap of the planet.

questions.question: The Dead Sea earned its name for what reason?

answers.text: Almost nothing can live in its salty water
A great battle once dyed it red with blood
An ancient city drowned beneath it

questions.fun_fact: Its extreme salinity, nearly ten times that of the ocean, kills off fish and plants, leaving the water 'dead'. Only a few hardy microbes manage to survive in it.

questions.question: The Caribbean Sea takes its name from what?

answers.text: The Carib people who lived in the region

questions.fun_fact: It is named for the Carib, an Indigenous people of the Lesser Antilles. The word 'cannibal' also derives from a Spanish rendering of their name, the result of disputed colonial-era accounts.

questions.question: The Sahara Desert's name is striking because in Arabic it essentially means what?
questions.fun_fact: 'Sahara' comes from the Arabic word for desert, so 'Sahara Desert' literally translates to 'Desert Desert'. Similar redundancies appear in names like the 'La Brea Tar Pits', which means 'the tar tar pits'.

questions.question: The Philippines was named in honour of whom?
questions.fun_fact: A Spanish expedition named the islands 'Las Islas Filipinas' in 1543 after the then-crown prince, the future Philip II. Magellan, who reached the islands first, has no country named after him at all.

questions.question: The English Channel separating England and France is called what in French?
questions.fun_fact: The French name 'La Manche' means 'the sleeve', a reference to the channel's long tapering shape. The two countries effectively named the same stretch of water after two completely different things.

questions.question: The country of Venezuela was named because early explorers thought a lakeside settlement resembled what city?
questions.fun_fact: Stilt houses over Lake Maracaibo reminded a 1499 Spanish expedition of Venice, so they named the land 'Venezuela', or 'little Venice'. A country was named after a passing resemblance to an Italian canal city.

questions.question: Iceland and Greenland are sometimes said to have 'swapped' the wrong names. Which one is actually greener?
questions.fun_fact: Iceland is far greener and warmer than its name suggests, thanks to the Gulf Stream, while Greenland is about 80% covered by ice sheet. The naming is a quirk of history, not geography.

questions.question: Wall Street in New York City got its name from what?

answers.text: An actual defensive wall built by Dutch settlers
A famous banker named Jan de Waal
The high stone walls of its first bank

questions.fun_fact: The Dutch built a wooden palisade wall along the northern edge of their settlement of New Amsterdam in the 1650s for defence. The wall is long gone, but the street tracing its line kept the name.

questions.question: The Bering Strait between Asia and North America is named after Vitus Bering, who was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Bering was a Danish-born navigator sailing in the service of the Russian Empire when he charted the strait in 1728. He later died of scurvy and exposure on an island that also now bears his name.

questions.question: The country of Argentina takes its name from a Latin word for which metal?
questions.fun_fact: 'Argentina' derives from 'argentum', Latin for silver, born of an early legend about a 'Sierra de la Plata', a mountain of silver. The metal proved a myth there, but the hopeful name endured.

questions.question: The Atlantic Ocean is named after what?

answers.text: Atlas, a titan of Greek mythology

questions.fun_fact: The name comes from 'Sea of Atlas', referring to the titan condemned to hold up the sky, who the Greeks placed near the Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa at the edge of their known world.

questions.question: Russia is so large that it covers roughly what fraction of all the land on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Russia spans about 17 million square kilometres, roughly 11% of Earth's land area. That single country is larger than the entire surface of the dwarf planet Pluto.

questions.question: Africa is so much bigger than it looks on most maps that you could fit the USA, China, and India inside it at once. True or false?

answers.text: False — it only fits the USA
False — Africa is smaller than China

questions.fun_fact: Africa is about 30 million square kilometres. The USA, China, and India combined cover roughly 25 million and would still fit inside it — the Mercator projection badly shrinks equatorial regions and inflates the poles.

questions.question: Which national park is this hot spring in?
questions.fun_fact: The colour rings of the Grand Prismatic Spring are mats of bacteria. Almost nothing survives the roughly 70 °C centre, so it stays clear and blue; the water cools towards the rim, and different microbes tint each temperature band yellow, orange and red.

questions.question: Which city is this statue in?
questions.fun_fact: The Statue of Liberty crossed the Atlantic from France in 1885 in 214 crates and was assembled on the island. Its copper skin is barely two millimetres thick — the iron framework inside carries the whole figure.

questions.question: Which strait separates Europe from Africa here?
questions.fun_fact: At its narrowest the strait is only about 14 kilometres across. The water swaps in two layers: less salty Atlantic water flows in on top, saltier Mediterranean water flows back out underneath.

questions.question: Which river is picked out here at night from space?
questions.fun_fact: Nearly everyone in Egypt lives on the narrow strip along the Nile and in its delta — a few percent of the country's area. That is why the band of light stops so abruptly where the desert starts.

questions.question: Which country is this building in?
questions.fun_fact: The Taj Mahal at Agra was begun in 1632 as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. This is a photochrom from around 1890: a black-and-white photograph whose colours were laid on by hand at the printing stage.
